I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I have $648 and a dark blue monopoly on Park Place and Boardwalk with one house on Boardwalk. I plan to mortgage Vermont Avenue for $50, then build houses on both properties to reach two houses each.

Only Park Place is buildable right now because of the even-build rule. Boardwalk has one house and Park Place has none. I must finish building before the turn ends.

I am weighing two paths. Building one house on Park Place now costs $200 and leaves $448. Mortgage Vermont next would give me $498, but that only covers the second house and leaves $98. I need to decide whether to build immediately or save cash first.

The build tool accepts multiple properties in one plan, but the engine likely enforces the even-build rule only on the final distribution. I will mortgage Vermont first to raise cash, then build both houses in a single action.

Building all three houses now would leave only $48. I cannot build on Boardwalk yet because the even-build rule requires Park Place to catch up first.

I decided against mortgaging Kentucky Avenue to keep it as a red monopoly blocker and emergency cash. Player three is on Water Works and will roll next, with roughly a 17% chance of hitting either dark blue property. Boardwalk with one house already costs $200 in rent.

Player three has $867 in cash and owns no monopolies. Boardwalk with two houses costs $600, which they can afford. Three houses would cost $1400 and could bankrupt them after mortgaging their three properties for only $260.

Player one also cannot pay a $1400 rent on Boardwalk with three houses. Their liquid assets total roughly $1174. Player four has $951 in cash.

Player four has roughly $1406 in liquid assets. A three-house Boardwalk would bankrupt them only after mortgaging everything, leaving about six dollars. The real danger is four houses on Boardwalk, which costs $1700. I will build two houses on both properties to reach the two-house level and avoid that risk.

Mortgaging Kentucky Avenue would raise enough cash to build four houses, but that leaves only about eight dollars. That is too risky because of upcoming rent, taxes, and chance or community chest cards. I am checking which opponents can charge me rent from my current position on Reading Railroad.

I mapped the standard Monopoly board to check which opponent properties I could land on from Reading Railroad. Rolling two through twelve spaces from space five would reach positions seven through seventeen, covering Oriental Avenue through St. Charles Place.

I have already moved this turn, so I will end it and let player three roll from Water Works. Player four rolls next from Tennessee, then player one from Connecticut, and I roll last. No opponent can land on my properties before my turn.

I will not end the turn with one house on Boardwalk. Player three can land there for only $200 or $35, which is too weak to force bankruptcy. Reaching two houses on both properties would cost $808 and leave me with just eight dollars. That is too risky. I am now checking which opponent properties I could land on from Reading Railroad on my next turn.

From Reading Railroad, rolling two spaces lands on Oriental Avenue, which costs only six dollars because player three owns no monopoly there. Rolling three spaces lands on a chance card, four on Vermont Avenue, five on Connecticut Avenue for eight dollars, and seven on St. Charles Place, which is mortgaged and collects no rent.

Player four's only active utility is Electric Company, so rolling there would cost thirty-two dollars. The rest of the route from Reading Railroad offers minimal rent exposure. Taxes are not a factor on this stretch. A bad chance card could still wipe the remaining eight dollars.

A "you have been elected chairman" chance card would cost one hundred fifty dollars. That is fatal with only eight dollars left. A "general repairs" card would cost one hundred twenty-five dollars with five houses. The chance of hitting a dangerous card from Reading Railroad is only two in thirty-six. Still, leaving that little cash is reckless.

The two-house plan is more robust than the four-house alternative. Two houses on Boardwalk and Park Place would leave roughly ninety-eight dollars, which is safer than the eight-dollar buffer. Player three would pay six hundred dollars and drop to about two hundred sixty-seven dollars. Player four would pay six hundred dollars and drop to about three hundred fifty-one dollars. Player one would pay six hundred dollars and drop to about sixty-four dollars. This applies meaningful pressure without leaving me broke.

I am now comparing BW2/PP1 with $248–298 cash against BW2/PP2 with $48–98 cash. The former leaves more buffer but weaker rent. I am checking player three's hit distribution from Water Works to decide.

Player three is twice as likely to land on Park Place as Boardwalk from Water Works. Adding a second house there would raise rent from one hundred seventy-five dollars to five hundred dollars, giving about thirty-six dollars in expected value for two hundred dollars spent. Two houses on both properties is the right long-term development level given the cash constraints. The ninety-eight dollar buffer remains sound. I am also checking whether trading would help, noting that player four owns the brown group and no one owns the Baltic group.

The light blue, red, and orange groups are split across three players. Completing any of them would be expensive. The pink group is also fragmented. The yellow group has four unowned properties. The green group is split between player one and player four. Only the dark blue group is fully mine.

The dark blue monopoly is the only viable win condition, so it must not be traded away. The other railroads are unowned or mortgaged by opponents and cannot be completed. Selling Vermont would not complete any color group alone, though it could help another player reach two of three light blues.

I will mortgage Vermont Avenue first. Building toward two houses on both dark blue properties is the certain next step. Trading is too uncertain and would waste time.

Vermont Avenue is a dead asset with no monopoly and only six dollars in rent. Its fifty-dollar mortgage value is worth keeping for the buffer, and the slight trade penalty is acceptable. Building Park Place first and then mortgaging Vermont would reach the same endpoint, so the order does not matter.
